# Execution Harnesses and Tool Isolation {#sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces}

![](images/ch06-cover-map.svg){fig-alt="Nested environment, harness, wrapper, and tool boundaries turn an authorized request into a complete execution record for later qualification."}

::: {.epigraph}
> "We shape our tools and thereafter they shape us."
>
> — John M. Culkin, "A Schoolman's Guide to Marshall McLuhan" (1967) [@Culkin1967Schoolman, p. 70]
:::

A design method needs a way to turn a proposed change or evaluation into work that architecture tools can perform. An execution environment provides that connection: it defines the actions a method can request, runs the appropriate tools on the intended design and workload, and returns observations, execution status, and cost. This lets a design loop use tool feedback to guide further work while keeping track of which candidate each result describes. Building such an environment requires coordinating inputs, tool state, and shared resources as requests run, fail, or resume.

This chapter explains how tools, wrappers, and harnesses contribute to that environment. It separates setup, which establishes inputs and interfaces, from runtime, which manages execution and recovery, and shows what must be retained with each result. The prospective Lighthouse mobile extended-reality (XR) system-on-chip (SoC) study illustrates these responsibilities; its execution examples are hypothetical, and its requests have not been dispatched. The environment establishes what ran and what returned. Determining what those observations support, and how they should guide verification and learning, is the subject of @sec-feedback-verification-trust.

## Environment Structure

Consider a method comparing the cache capacities introduced in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization. It requests an evaluation of one candidate under a specified workload. The environment checks the request, translates the candidate into the simulator's configuration, and arranges execution with the required resources. When the run ends, it returns the available observations together with the execution status, conditions, and cost. The method can then decide what work to request next. The simulator performs the modeled execution; the surrounding environment connects that execution to the design process.

Now suppose the simulation stops halfway through and a script launches it again. Before interpreting the new result, we need to know whether the second run used the same candidate and workload, started fresh or resumed a checkpoint, and stayed within the remaining budget. Any partial output and cost from the first attempt still belong to the study. Restarting a command does not by itself preserve those connections. The environment must control what state the new attempt inherits and retain the relationship between the attempts.

An environment therefore defines both an interface for the method and the execution conditions behind that interface. The interface specifies what actions can be requested and what information comes back. The execution mechanisms manage the tools, workspaces, and resources needed to carry out those actions. In an interactive computer-aided design (CAD) workflow, an engineer may perform much of this coordination manually. Automated loops need to provide it as requests accumulate and several candidates are in progress at once.[^fn-sandboxing-kubernetes-c06] Distinguishing the components that perform this work makes it easier to build a small environment first and extend it as the study requires.

### From Tools to an Execution Environment

A method interacts with the environment through requests and returned observations. Inside that environment, several components connect those requests to executable work. Five terms distinguish their responsibilities; they do not describe five independent layers that every system must implement.

- **Tool**: Performs a transformation or analysis, such as compiling software with LLVM, synthesizing a design with Yosys, or analyzing timing with OpenSTA. It consumes inputs in its own formats and produces artifacts or reports.
- **Simulator**: A type of tool that executes a model of hardware or software behavior. For example, gem5 can supply observations from a configured microarchitectural model. Those observations describe the modeled system under the supplied conditions.
- **Wrapper**: Adapts a tool to the environment's interface. It validates a request, translates it into tool inputs, invokes the tool, and parses the returned material while retaining the original reports.
- **Harness**: Coordinates execution across requests and tools. It manages dependencies, tracks running work, and handles failures, retries, and resource use while keeping each result associated with its inputs.
- **Environment**: Combines the accessible design state, permitted actions, tool interfaces, and execution mechanisms into the system the method can use. It determines what the method can inspect, change, and evaluate, and what information it receives afterward.

Suppose a generator proposes revised controller code and requests a behavioral check. The wrapper supplies the identified code and test inputs to a simulator and returns its status and outputs in a form the caller can use. The harness tracks that attempt and any dependent work, such as synthesis of a candidate that passes the initial checks. The environment defines whether the caller may submit a new implementation, alter a constraint, or only evaluate an existing artifact. Supporting generated designs therefore requires accepting identified artifacts and their matching inputs, rather than exposing only parameter changes to one fixed model.

A small script may perform both wrapping and coordination. An engineer running a few tools manually may need only simple scripts and retained inputs and reports. A closed-loop optimizer needs automated tracking as requests accumulate; a system coordinating redesign across tools must also preserve the relationships between new artifacts and their evaluations (@fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration). The implementation can grow with the work while keeping these responsibilities clear.

Existing electronic design automation (EDA) frameworks provide useful building blocks. SiliconCompiler connects design data, tool settings, and process design kit (PDK) information through a shared schema and execution flow [@SiliconCompiler]. Hammer separates tool-specific steps, technology information, and project configuration through its plugin interfaces [@Hammer]. Such frameworks supply reusable hardware-flow knowledge; a study must still define which actions its methods can request and how returned results enter the design loop. General build and scheduling systems can support execution as well, provided the surrounding integration preserves the required design and tool information.

Submission volume and reliable automated execution are different observations. The cumulative shuttle counts in @fig-api-driven-tapeouts come from an unverified transcription attributed to open-access programs; they do not establish how much design work was automated, what manual intervention remained, or whether the flows operated reliably. Evaluating those claims would require execution records and a consistent definition of automated work. For environment design, the practical issue is the work admitted concurrently and the resources it shares, which the host and network controls below must manage.

![**Unverified cumulative submission counts across open-access shuttle runs.** The underlying transcription attributes counts to Efabless Open multi-project wafer (MPW) and Tiny Tapeout shuttles, reaching 1,827 cumulative submissions in September 2024 from 45 in December 2020. These are cumulative entries, not annual totals. Row-level source traceability is incomplete; the plot's designation of these entries as programmatic tapeouts is not independently established. The series does not measure automation quality or operational viability.](images/plot_ch6.png){#fig-api-driven-tapeouts width="80%" fig-alt="Line plot of unverified cumulative shuttle submission counts from 45 in December 2020 to 1,827 in September 2024. The original axis labels the entries programmatic tapeouts, a classification not established by the retained source data."}

### Host and Network Boundaries

An evaluation request runs on a host with finite resources and access to project data. Several requests may share licenses, processors, and storage, while a generated script can affect whatever its process can reach. The environment therefore needs to control both resource sharing and access. Five concerns illustrate what this means for hardware tools; the appropriate mechanisms depend on the tools, deployment, and study restrictions.

1. **Shared licenses.** Commercial EDA tools often require a license checkout before work can proceed. License managers such as FlexLM[^fn-flexlm-c06] and Sentinel manage this shared capacity. Launching more workers cannot increase it: an automated loop can occupy available licenses and leave other work waiting. The harness tracks each request's license requirements alongside its compute requirements, queues work when capacity is unavailable, and monitors checkout status. A local token pool coordinates the harness's own requests, but it does not reserve capacity against other users. After a worker fails, recovery must follow the license server's supported timeout and reclamation policy; a terminated process is not sufficient evidence that its license is available again.

2. **Restricted data.** A study may permit an external model to propose design changes while requiring foundry models and proprietary design files to remain on approved hosts. The environment must enforce those restrictions for process design kit (PDK) collateral, layout views, transistor-level models, and any derived information covered by the study's disclosure policy. A proxy can mediate requests between an external model and internal tools, but its return interface needs equal attention. Replacing absolute delays with "Path A is 12% slower than Path B," or removing die coordinates from a congestion map, reduces detail without establishing that the result may be disclosed. Prompts and abstract syntax tree (AST) edits can also contain proprietary information. The environment needs an explicit definition of what may cross this boundary, including feedback from synthesis, design rule checking (DRC), and layout versus schematic (LVS) checks.

3. **Host runtime variation.** A simulator's elapsed time depends on the machine running it as well as the modeled design. Worker migration across non-uniform memory access (NUMA) nodes, competing memory traffic, and central processing unit (CPU) frequency changes can alter execution time and throughput. Where runtime comparisons matter, controlled resource allocation helps make those comparisons interpretable. On Linux, CPU affinity tools such as `taskset -c` can restrict where threads run; scheduling must separately prevent unwanted contention on those cores. CPU frequency policies and storage placement may also need control. RAM-backed temporary storage such as `/dev/shm` or tmpfs is useful only when its memory demands fit the allocation. These choices can reduce host interference, but they do not make a nondeterministic tool deterministic. @sec-incremental-churn-dispersion separates host timing variation from changes in returned design results.

4. **Generated scripts and host access.** A synthesis script is executable input. Tcl commands such as `exec` and pipeline forms of `open` can launch programs with the permissions available to the tool process. A generated script can therefore overwrite files or make network requests beyond the intended design operation. The environment should give execution only the files, permissions, and network access needed for that operation. One implementation uses unprivileged Open Container Initiative (OCI) containers, user namespaces, read-only library and PDK mounts, and restricted network access. System-call filters such as seccomp can further limit available kernel operations. These mechanisms address different parts of isolation: filesystem protection still depends on exposed mounts and permissions, and a container alone does not establish the required boundary.

5. **Storage and retained artifacts.** Physical design tools produce large databases, checkpoints, and exchange files, including Synopsys NDM databases, DEF layout data, Standard Parasitic Exchange Format (SPEF) parasitics, and GDSII streams.[^fn-physical-checkpoints-c06] Concurrent writes can saturate shared storage and leave otherwise available processors waiting. Local scratch storage can absorb active writes, but the environment must move needed outputs to persistent storage before reclaiming a workspace. What must remain depends on subsequent work: a parser failure may require raw reports, a resumed run needs its checkpoint, and result review may require more than extracted metrics. Failed or filtered candidates still need the material required for their recovery and review. Large intermediates can be removed once those uses no longer require them, with the retained record stating what remains available.

### Tool Wrappers

Host and network controls determine where execution can occur and what it can access. A wrapper connects the method's request to the tool running within those limits. Suppose a generator submits revised controller code for synthesis under a specified clock constraint and cell library. If the tool uses a default clock period or a different library, it answers a different question even if it exits successfully. The wrapper must translate the request explicitly and report any mismatch it can detect. If it cannot express a required setting through the tool's interface, it should refuse the request rather than silently substitute another setting.

Before launch, the wrapper checks that the request contains the required fields, identifies available inputs, and uses supported parameter values. For the controller, this includes resolving the intended source files and library and preparing the clock constraint in Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) form. These checks have different purposes: a numeric parameter must lie within its allowed range, whereas an artifact identifier must resolve to the intended input. A request can pass these checks and still describe a faulty design or encounter a tool failure. Validation catches detectable input problems before expensive execution; it does not establish design correctness.

The return path needs similar care. Execution yields a status and any reports or design artifacts the tool produced. A parser extracts named quantities, their units, and relevant conditions from the reports while preserving the raw material. The harness associates these outputs with the request and execution attempt and records resource use. @fig-environment-tool-interface follows this path from a typed request, whose fields have defined types and requirements, through execution to a recorded result. Keeping execution status separate from parsing status lets the caller distinguish a failed run from a completed run whose output could not be fully read.

![**Tool wrappers separate raw execution state from semantic result interpretation.** The wrapper validates and translates incoming typed requests before invoking backend tools; the isolated tool executes declared operations; the parser extracts structured attributes while retaining unclassified residual output; and the harness binds runtime outcomes, parse statuses, compute costs, and lineage into immutable execution records.](images/fig-environment-tool-interface){#fig-environment-tool-interface width="80%" fig-alt="An architecture question and workload, action schema, constraints, and metric definitions enter the tool-connected environment as a typed request. The wrapper validates and translates the request before calling the tool. An invalid request goes directly to the harness record. The tool separately produces raw returned material and a runtime outcome that can be failed, partial, or complete. The parser turns retained raw material into structured attributes, unclassified residual output, and a parse status. The harness records request and attempt identity, conditions, runtime outcome, artifacts, parse status, cost, and lineage."}

For the synthesis request, the wrapper might return a mapped netlist and timing information under the requested constraints. Other wrappers may extract gem5 miss rates or power estimates derived from switching activity. Each interface must define which outputs it requires and how it reports missing or partial results. An absent metric must remain distinguishable from a measured zero. Warnings and unrecognized log lines also need to remain available: an unconstrained timing endpoint, for example, may affect how a reported timing result should be interpreted.

This is the distinction between parsing a report and deciding what it supports. A structured return makes tool feedback usable by a method, but does not by itself establish that the evaluation answers the architectural question. The wrapper checks and reports what its interface can establish; later analysis can examine the retained outputs and conditions. Even an explicit request and a careful parser are insufficient if the tool inherits unintended state from an earlier run. Controlling that state is the next part of preserving the request's meaning.

### Stateful Tools and Exact Translation

A tool's starting state is part of its input, even when that state is absent from the request. A physical design session may already contain a netlist, placement, and routing data; a simulator may resume from a checkpoint. For example, OpenROAD can save and reload its design database [@OpenROADDocs]. If a generator submits revised controller code but execution resumes from a database built from the previous version, the resulting report may describe the old design. Correctly parsing that report cannot repair the mismatch.

Starting a fresh process in a clean workspace is one way to control inherited state, provided it loads the intended inputs and environment settings. Reusing a session or checkpoint can save work, but the environment must establish what state is being reused and whether it is suitable for the next operation. A reset must restore the required starting state; a deliberate continuation must identify its checkpoint and prior work. Temporary files, in-memory databases, and inherited environment variables all matter when they can affect execution. The aim is to make reuse explicit and checkable, rather than require a new process for every invocation.

The same problem extends across tools because a candidate has several representations. Register-transfer level (RTL) code describes behavior, while synthesis produces a netlist mapped to a cell library. Yosys, for example, can map logic to cells described by a target library [@Yosys]. Physical implementation then needs the matching library information: Liberty (`.lib`) files supply timing and power characterization, while Library Exchange Format (LEF) files describe physical abstractions used during layout. OpenROAD consumes these inputs alongside the design [@OpenROADDocs]. A power-aware flow also needs applicable power intent. Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 1801 Unified Power Format (UPF) describes matters such as power domains and isolation requirements; it does not itself estimate power.[^fn-eda-formats-c06]

These files must describe compatible design and operating assumptions. If a generator changes a block's interface, an old physical abstraction may no longer match it. If an analysis loads a library characterized at 0.75\ V when the request specifies another voltage, the returned timing and power describe different conditions. A change in power domains may also require updated power intent. The environment must track which inputs each tool path depends on and check their compatibility before using its results. Merely collecting files under the same candidate identifier does not establish that they belong together.

Translation introduces a related obligation. A wrapper may convert units or express a setting in a tool's syntax, but it must preserve the requested value and meaning. Silently rounding a capacity or changing an array dimension creates a different candidate. Different tools may legitimately use different abstractions of that candidate, provided the modeled properties and limitations are explicit. When a backend cannot represent a required feature, the wrapper should return that limitation so the design loop can choose another evaluation path. Changing the candidate to make execution succeed is a new design proposal, not a translation repair.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="One XR SoC request, several tool representations"}
**Context.** The prospective Lighthouse study illustrates how one candidate can require different tool inputs without changing the design under comparison.

**Application.** Consider a candidate with a 3\ MiB cache, a neural processing unit (NPU) array ($16 \times 16$), and dual LPDDR5X channels. An analytical model would use the dimensions and process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) assumptions relevant to its estimates. A configured gem5 model would represent the supported timing behavior, while a Verilator-based path would execute the supplied RTL and testbench. Each path would need matching workload inputs or traffic generators and an explicit account of which candidate features it represents.

**Required behavior.** Wrappers must preserve relevant capacities, dimensions, cache policies, and memory arbitration wherever those properties are modeled. An unsupported feature must be reported rather than silently replaced by a default. Differences between tool outputs must be interpreted in light of their models and conditions. These are requirements for the unexecuted study, not observed wrapper results.
:::

## Environment Setup

Before methods can use an environment, we need to establish how it accepts work and keeps track of what runs. Setup defines how design artifacts and their dependencies are identified, what requests each tool interface accepts and returns, and which evaluation paths are available for the properties of interest. Those paths may support behavioral checks, performance estimates, or physical implementation, depending on the study.

The candidates themselves need not all exist at setup time. A generator may produce new controller code during the design loop; the environment needs an established way to register that artifact, associate it with its inputs, and pass it to the appropriate tools. For each execution attempt, the inputs and conditions must be identified so that its outputs can be traced to the work performed. Runtime then manages the execution of that work. The first setup question is therefore how to preserve these relationships as designs and tool outputs accumulate.

### Lineage and Reproducibility

When a design changes, we need to know which existing artifacts still apply and which must be regenerated. *Lineage* records the history linking requests, transformations, and artifacts: which inputs produced an output, which candidate an evaluation used, and how a retry relates to an earlier attempt. Setup establishes how these relationships will be recorded as work proceeds. Retained input versions, such as source snapshots, constraints, and library files, remain separate from mutable working files so that later edits do not erase what an earlier run used.

Compilation and hardware elaboration turn source descriptions into representations that downstream tools can consume, including abstract syntax trees, control-data flow graphs (CDFGs), and gate netlists. A transformation record connects its output to the inputs and settings used to produce it. The useful information includes:

- Parent candidate and request identifiers, including the originating attempt when work is retried.
- Transformation tool and compiler versions, together with the settings used.
- Input and output content hashes, which identify the retained file contents.
- Applicable operating conditions and references to the required libraries or models.
- Checks performed on the transformation, their outcomes, and any properties left unchecked.
- Downstream uses permitted by the study, including any restrictions on the resulting artifacts.

These records form a dependency graph. Suppose a parameter in a high-level C++ hardware model changes. Artifacts derived from that parameter, such as generated RTL and its synthesized netlist, must be regenerated or otherwise shown to remain applicable before reuse. A software testbench can remain unchanged only if it does not depend on the changed behavior or interface. If the same parameter determines its expected outputs, the testbench is affected too. Selective rebuilding works only when the recorded dependencies include the inputs that actually influence each transformation.

@fig-artifact-lineage illustrates this reasoning with separate software compilation and hardware elaboration paths. The evaluation brings their outputs together with a workload, tool version, and operating conditions. Keeping versioned artifacts and their transformations in a directed acyclic graph allows a later design revision to add a new path while preserving the history of earlier evaluations.

![**Evaluated software and hardware artifacts retain explicit parent transformation lineage.** A single architectural intent branches into parallel software compilation and hardware elaboration paths. Each intermediate artifact (binary executable, Verilog RTL, gate netlist) inherits cryptographic parent hashes, tool versions, and operating conditions. Modifying any upstream input or configuration generates a distinct evaluation identity rather than overwriting existing records.](images/fig-artifact-lineage){#fig-artifact-lineage width="80%" fig-alt="A single Lighthouse intent branches into a software variant and a hardware variant. The software compiles into an identified binary, and the hardware elaborates into an identified RTL artifact. An evaluation instance binds both artifacts to the tool and version, workload, and operating conditions. Hashes and evaluation keys distinguish exact artifacts and paths but do not prove functional equivalence or reproducibility."}

An evaluation key identifies the combination being evaluated. It can incorporate content hashes of the design artifacts and workload, tool and container versions, and relevant settings. The environment must construct the key from all declared inputs that distinguish evaluations; recording parent hashes alone does not discover a missing dependency. A changed compiler version can produce a new evaluation key even if the output binary is unchanged. Conversely, repeated executions of the same identified configuration still need separate attempt records, because their outcomes and costs may differ.

Conditions belong in this history as well. For physical timing, a slack of -12\ ps at a slow corner and the same value at a typical corner describe different operating cases. They can be compared with those conditions in view, but cannot be treated as interchangeable observations. Software measurements also depend on details beyond the source program: experiments have shown that link order and environment-variable layout can bias performance comparisons [@Mytkowicz2009WrongData]. The practical lesson is to retain the execution conditions that can affect the property being measured.

Lineage makes an evaluation traceable and supplies information needed to repeat it. It does not prove that a transformation preserved behavior or that another execution will reproduce the result. Those questions require the relevant checks, accessible artifacts, and a working execution procedure. Similarly, records can help determine whether a checkpoint belongs to the requested configuration, but the tool's resume protocol must still establish the intended starting state. Once these identities and dependencies are defined, tool interfaces can carry them consistently through requests and returns.

### Typed Tool Interfaces

The interface defines the actions a method can take. During setup, we specify each action's inputs, permitted changes, preconditions, and returned information. Types make these requirements explicit: a reference to source code, a clock period with units, and an execution-time limit serve different purposes even if a command-line tool ultimately receives them all as text. The interface must also define what those fields mean and how they relate. Type checking alone cannot establish that a library matches a design or that a requested analysis is appropriate.

For the controller example, an environment might expose separate actions to submit an implementation, synthesize an identified version, and evaluate its timing. A synthesis request would identify the source artifact, top-level module, library, and constraints; its return would identify any generated netlist and reports alongside execution and parsing status. If the study holds the library fixed, the interface should resolve that setting from the study configuration and reject conflicting requests. Accepting a new implementation allows a generator to revise the design within the study's scope. An interface limited to selecting values for predefined parameters permits a narrower kind of design change.

Across the tool classes in @tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum, interfaces can share fields for request identifiers, execution status, output references, cost, and error information. Submission and cancellation behavior can also follow common conventions. Tool-specific inputs and outputs still need their own definitions. Interfaces to synthesis with Yosys and physical implementation with OpenROAD, for example, must accommodate the different artifacts and constraints those operations require [@Yosys; @AjayiEtAl2019OpenROAD]. A timing slack and an architectural simulator's instructions per cycle (IPC) estimate cannot become interchangeable simply because both are returned as numeric fields. An adapter for a commercial tool likewise has to account for that tool's capabilities, formats, and access restrictions.

When an action changes design structure, a structured intermediate representation (IR) can make the allowed transformation easier to express and check. Circuit IR Compilers and Tools (CIRCT) builds on Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) and provides dialects, or sets of operations and types, for hardware descriptions. Its `hw`, `comb`, and `seq` dialects represent module structure, combinational logic, and sequential elements [@CIRCT]. An interface can use these structures to identify the operation or module to change instead of relying on text substitution alone. A well-formed representation still requires appropriate behavioral checks after a change; structural validity does not establish that the revised design meets its specification.

The interface implementation needs testing before a method relies on it. Small fixtures pair requests with expected tool inputs and representative reports with expected parsed returns. Tests should cover unit conversion, unsupported settings, and missing outputs as well as successful requests. Failure injection exercises cases such as timeouts, terminated processes, and truncated reports to check whether the interface returns the promised status and retains useful diagnostics. Systematic recovery testing has precedent in distributed systems, including FATE and DESTINI [@GunawiEtAl2011FATEDestini]; the failures and expected responses here must be chosen for the hardware tool path. With the actions and their behavior defined, the next question is which combination of tools can evaluate the properties the study needs.

### Multi-Tool Toolchains and Fidelity

A revised controller raises several questions: does it behave correctly, how does it affect workload execution, and can its implementation meet timing? Different tools address different parts of that evaluation. @sec-data-representations-world-models explains which sources reveal which properties; here we need to connect those sources into executable tool paths. Each path requires its own inputs, model assumptions, and outputs, even when it starts from the same candidate.

Fidelity describes how well a model represents the property under study. It is not a universal ranking of tools. An RTL simulation can expose behavior that an analytical model omits, while a physical timing analysis addresses delays that an unannotated RTL simulation does not model. A formal check answers a specified correctness question under its assumptions. Greater detail in one of these evaluations does not replace the others.

A study can still stage its work economically. Fast estimates may screen candidates before more expensive evaluations, provided the screening method is suitable for the property and operating range. Other checks may run in parallel because they answer independent questions. @tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum summarizes these complementary tool classes and the state each path must retain. Its rows are not a sequence that every candidate must traverse.

| **Tool class** | **Representative use** | **What it models or checks** | **Preserved environment state** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Analytical / circuit model | CACTI, spreadsheet models [@MuralimanoharEtAl2009CACTI]. | Analytical equations and technology assumptions without workload execution. | Model version, macro geometry, PVT conditions, technology limits. |
| Compiler and build stack | TVM, IREE, LLVM pass pipelines, linkers. | Generation of executable binaries; no hardware timing. | Source intermediate representations (IRs), target instruction set architecture (ISA) flags, compiler versions, binary hashes. |
| Functional ISA emulator | Spike, QEMU ISA execution. | Instruction semantics without microarchitectural timing. | Target binary, ISA extensions, input state, functional output. |
| Timing simulation | gem5 [@BinkertEtAl2011Gem5], SST, Ramulator 2, SCALE-Sim. | Pipeline, cache, network-on-chip (NoC), memory controller, and accelerator timing. | Workload inputs, traces, warmup length, seeds, event traces. |
| RTL simulation / testbench | Verilator [@Veripool2026Verilator], cocotb, Synopsys VCS. | Cycle behavior under RTL semantics; no routed delay unless annotated. | RTL hash, testbench, compile flags, waveform traces. |
| Formal verification | SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) and bounded model checking (BMC) via SymbiYosys or JasperGold [@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. | Stated invariants/relations under declared proof methods and bounds. | Property definitions, bounds, solver engine, proof certificates. |
| Emulation and field-programmable gate array (FPGA) | ZeBu, Palladium, FireSim on cloud FPGAs [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. | Accelerated target execution. FPGA mapping is not application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) signoff. | Target bitstream, host allocation, workload snapshot, traces. |
| Physical implementation / timing analysis | OpenROAD implementation flow; OpenSTA timing analysis [@OpenROADDocs]. | Placement, routing, and modeled timing under supplied libraries, parasitics, and constraints. | Netlist, library/PDK views, SDC constraints, layout and parasitic artifacts, operating corners, stage settings. |
: **Fidelity is relative to the property under evaluation.** Harnesses preserve model assumptions, inputs, stages, and artifacts rather than collapsing returns into scalar scores. {#tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum tbl-colwidths="[20,24,28,28]"}

The meaning of a return depends on how the tool was used. A formal result must identify the property and assumptions, and distinguish bounded checking from an inductive proof such as $k$-induction.[^fn-k-induction-c06] A completed bounded check does not establish behavior beyond its bound. This information belongs with the result so that the next method can use it within its scope.

Sampling introduces another kind of qualification. SimPoint and SMARTS[^fn-simpoint-smarts-c06] let simulators evaluate selected intervals and estimate the full workload's behavior [@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint; @WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. The environment must retain the interval-selection method, applicable weights, warmup choices, and any checkpoint dependencies. These identify what execution was sampled and how its observations contribute to the estimate.

A shared design configuration helps connect the paths. Chipyard, an SoC development framework, brings software simulation, physical implementation, and FPGA-accelerated simulation into a common design ecosystem [@chipyard]. @fig-chipyard-framework shows a simplified flow from configuration through hardware generation into those toolchains. Branch-specific settings and transformations still need to be recorded; a common starting configuration alone does not establish that every backend evaluates identical behavior.

![**Unified design configurations anchor multi-tool evaluation flows.** In this architectural flow based on the Chipyard (a widely used academic SoC generator) SoC framework [@chipyard], a single root configuration lowers through Chisel generation and FIRRTL transformations before fanning out into specialized evaluation toolchains: software RTL simulation (Verilator/Synopsys VCS), very-large-scale integration (VLSI) physical design (OpenROAD), and FPGA-accelerated simulation (FireSim). Shared configuration lineage preserves parameter traceability across fidelity tiers without conflating distinct physical returns.](images/fig-chipyard-framework){#fig-chipyard-framework width="80%" fig-alt="A simplified flow diagram of the Chipyard (a widely used academic SoC generator) paths described by the cited framework. A common configuration feeds Chisel generation and compiler transformations. Branch-specific tools then produce artifacts for RTL simulation, a VLSI implementation flow, and FPGA-accelerated simulation."}

Shared configuration history helps us trace a result back to a candidate, but the outputs retain the meaning of their evaluation path. Cycle counts from an unannotated Verilator testbench cannot substitute for post-route timing slack, and FPGA execution rates are not ASIC clock frequencies. Likewise, FPGA resource utilization may reward a design that maps efficiently to lookup tables without establishing its standard-cell area. Using such a quantity as a predictor requires evidence for that relationship. The environment must retain the tool, model, conditions, and units with each metric so the method can distinguish these uses.

Throughput also depends on the configuration being evaluated. ZSim reports about 20\ MIPS (million instructions per second) per simulated core, with about $200\times$ slowdown for its detailed out-of-order model [@ZSim]. The FireSim paper reports a 1,024-node target cluster running at a simulated processor clock rate of 3.4\ MHz, less than $1{,}000\times$ slower than its 3.2\ GHz target [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. These are results for different modeled systems, not a direct performance comparison. Instructions per second and target cycles per second count different work; the reported slowdown factors also depend on their respective reference systems.

@fig-ch06-simulation-spectrum pairs each execution path with a reporting unit and the conditions that comparisons must match. After selecting a tool that observes the required property, the environment can budget its work in those units. Preparing a compiled simulator or FPGA image also consumes time, so the execution plan must distinguish preparation cost from the cost of subsequent runs that reuse it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ch06-simulation-spectrum
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Throughput comparisons require a declared unit of work.**
#|   Different execution paths count different work: model evaluations, instructions, target cycles, properties, or
#|   physical flow stages. The final column identifies conditions needed before even two rates in the same row can
#|   be compared. Row order implies no throughput or fidelity ranking. Author-constructed comparison guide, not a
#|   measured benchmark.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Comparison guide pairing six execution paths with units for reporting work and the conditions that comparisons must match. Model evaluations, instructions, simulated or emulated target cycles, formal properties, and physical stages have distinct units; no shared numerical rate is shown."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

rows = [
    ["Analytical model", "Model evaluations / second", "Model, candidate size, host"],
    ["ISA execution", "Instructions / second", "ISA, workload, host"],
    ["Timing / RTL simulation", "Target cycles / host second", "Target model, workload, host"],
    ["Hardware emulation", "Target cycles / host second", "Mapped target, workload, testbed"],
    ["Formal verification", "Elapsed time / named property", "Property, model, bound, solver"],
    ["Physical implementation", "Elapsed time / defined stage", "Design, libraries, stage settings"],
]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.0, 3.25))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.97, bottom=0.03)
ax.axis("off")
table = ax.table(
    cellText=rows,
    colLabels=["Execution path", "Unit of work or elapsed time", "Conditions to match"],
    colWidths=[0.29, 0.35, 0.36],
    cellLoc="left", colLoc="left", bbox=[0, 0, 1, 1],
)
table.auto_set_font_size(False)
table.set_fontsize(7.0)
for (row, col), cell in table.get_celld().items():
    cell.set_edgecolor(COLORS["grid"])
    cell.set_linewidth(0.5)
    cell.PAD = 0.055
    cell.get_text().set_color(COLORS["ink"])
    if row == 0:
        cell.set_facecolor(COLORS["note_fill"])
        cell.get_text().set_weight("bold")
    else:
        cell.set_facecolor("white")
```

Frameworks provide different parts of this integration. ArchGym connects search algorithms to architecture simulators [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym], while CHIA supports co-design loops that combine design tools, simulators, software builds, and model calls [@CuiEtAl2026CHIA]. Workflow engines such as Nextflow and Snakemake can manage execution dependencies [@DiTommasoEtAl2017Nextflow; @KosterEtAl2012Snakemake]. The study still has to specify which tool path answers each question, which artifacts pass between stages, and what conditions permit reuse. Once those paths are configured, the harness must manage their execution as requests queue, run, and return.

## Environment Runtime

Runtime puts the configured tool paths into operation. It admits requests when resources are available, tracks work in progress, and returns outputs together with execution status and cost. Tools may create artifacts, update working files, or resume from checkpoints. Throughout those changes, the harness must keep each attempt associated with the inputs and conditions it actually used, including any intentional continuation of earlier work.

A design loop may propose another candidate while an earlier evaluation is still running. The new design must not overwrite inputs being used by that evaluation, and an interruption must not erase the work already performed. An asynchronous interface lets the caller submit work and return to it later, while the harness tracks unfinished attempts. This separation makes it possible to coordinate several candidates, handle failures, and decide when completed work can be reused. The first question is how to submit and monitor execution without accidentally launching the same work twice.

### Asynchronous Scheduling and Idempotency

A synchronous interface returns the result of an action through the call that requested it. The `step()` interface in reinforcement learning (RL) environments such as Gymnasium follows this pattern [@TowersEtAl2023Gymnasium]. It is convenient when evaluations finish quickly. For long-running architecture work, separating submission from completion lets a method monitor outstanding requests and continue other work while tools execute. A scheduler adapter connects the harness to an execution backend, such as Slurm, IBM LSF, or a container service.

The harness must distinguish what was requested from how it executes. A request describes the work; an attempt records one effort to carry it out; backend jobs perform that work. @fig-runtime-object-state shows why these are separate. A refused request can have an attempt record without launching a job. An admitted request may need one job or several, such as tests running in parallel. Their outputs, status, and costs belong to the same attempt. A deliberate retry after failure creates a new attempt linked to the previous one.

![**A single execution record tracks zero, one, or multiple backend tool executions.** The execution record anchors all backend tool executions to the authorized request, whether the request is refused prior to execution, creates a single tool job, or spawns multiple parallel execution segments. The record preserves returned raw artifacts, realized compute and license costs, and independent status attributes including scheduling state, terminal cause, parser health, and retry parent links. Conceptual runtime state schema.](images/fig-runtime-object-state){#fig-runtime-object-state width="80%" fig-alt="An authorized request creates one attempt. The attempt may be refused before a backend job exists, may create one job, or may create several jobs or execution segments. All paths feed one execution record. The execution record points separately to returned artifacts and realized cost. Scheduling state, terminal cause, artifact completeness, parser status, cancellation confirmation, and retry parent remain independent attributes."}

An attempt record must survive the processes that perform its work. If a scheduler preempts a simulation, the harness retains available logs and records the resources already consumed. A scheduler may requeue the job under the same attempt, in which case each execution segment remains part of its history. If the harness instead starts a new recovery attempt, it links that attempt to its predecessor. Neither path should erase the interruption or the earlier cost.

Now suppose the harness accepts a submission, but its reply never reaches the caller. Sending the request again must not launch another copy of the work. An *idempotent* submission has the same effect when repeated: the caller supplies the same `submission_token`, and the harness returns the existing attempt rather than creating another [@Featonby2021IdempotentAPIs]. Reusing that token with changed request contents should be rejected. A deliberate retry of failed work uses a new token and creates a linked attempt; it is different from retransmitting a submission whose outcome is unknown.

Providing this behavior requires more than attaching a token. The harness must retain the association among the token, request, attempt, and backend jobs. If it crashes during dispatch, recovery must determine whether work already exists before launching it again. When that cannot yet be established, the submission remains unresolved rather than being treated as evidence that no job started.

The interface in @lst-harness-interface separates these operations. `submit` returns an attempt identifier and admission status; `poll` reports progress; `collect` retrieves the execution record once the attempt reaches a terminal state, including any partial outputs and failures. When several jobs belong to an attempt, the harness must define how their states determine the attempt's status. One completed job cannot by itself establish that the whole attempt is complete. `cancel` requests termination, which must be confirmed for all attached work.

@fig-job-lifecycle illustrates common backend job transitions, including preemption and requeueing. It is a simplified view of a job, not the complete attempt interface: refusal before launch and cancellation are also represented in the listing. A completed job means execution ended, while parsing status and returned evidence still determine what information is available to the method.

```{python}
#| label: fig-job-lifecycle
#| fig-cap: "**Asynchronous job lifecycle.** A backend job progresses through explicit scheduling states. Preempted runs can queue again if policy permits; the execution record retains every execution segment. A new retry attempt links back to its predecessor. Terminal states finalize the relevant execution entries. Author-constructed illustrative diagram."
#| fig-alt: "State machine diagram showing a job moving from Queued to Running, and then to terminal states Completed or Failed, or to Evicted which can cycle back to Queued."
#| out-width: "100%"

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as patches
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 2.5))
ax.axis("off")
ax.set_xlim(0, 10)
ax.set_ylim(0, 4)

states = {
    "Queued": (2, 2.5),
    "Running": (5, 2.5),
    "Completed": (8, 3.5),
    "Failed": (8, 2.5),
    "Evicted": (8, 1.5),
}

# Draw nodes
for name, (x, y) in states.items():
    ax.text(x, y, name, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8, fontweight="bold",
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.6", facecolor=COLORS["note_fill"],
                      edgecolor=COLORS["ink"], linewidth=1.2), zorder=3)

# Draw edges
def draw_edge(start, end, label, offset_y=0, rad=0.0):
    x1, y1 = states[start]
    x2, y2 = states[end]
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x2, y2), xytext=(x1, y1),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["ink"], linewidth=1.2,
                                connectionstyle=f"arc3,rad={rad}", shrinkA=15, shrinkB=15), zorder=2)

    # Place label
    if start == "Queued" and end == "Running":
        ax.text((x1+x2)/2, (y1+y2)/2 + 0.15, label, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6, color=COLORS["ink"])
    elif start == "Running" and end == "Completed":
        ax.text((x1+x2)/2 - 0.2, (y1+y2)/2 + 0.15, label, ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=6, color=COLORS["ink"], rotation=15)
    elif start == "Running" and end == "Failed":
        ax.text((x1+x2)/2, (y1+y2)/2 + 0.15, label, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6, color=COLORS["ink"])
    elif start == "Running" and end == "Evicted":
        ax.text((x1+x2)/2 - 0.2, (y1+y2)/2 - 0.15, label, ha="right", va="top", fontsize=6, color=COLORS["ink"], rotation=-15)
    elif start == "Evicted" and end == "Queued":
        # Evicted to Queued curve
        ax.text((x1+x2)/2, (y1+y2)/2 - 0.8, label, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=6, color=COLORS["ink"])

draw_edge("Queued", "Running", "Allocate resources")
draw_edge("Running", "Completed", "Tool exits cleanly")
draw_edge("Running", "Failed", "Tool crashes or times out")
draw_edge("Running", "Evicted", "Scheduler preemption")
draw_edge("Evicted", "Queued", "Retry policy allows", rad=-0.3)

# Submit edge
ax.annotate("", xy=states["Queued"], xytext=(0, 2.5),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["ink"], linewidth=1.2, shrinkB=15), zorder=2)
ax.text(1, 2.65, "Submit request", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6, color=COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
```

```{.yaml #lst-harness-interface lst-cap="**Harness interface shape.** Three normal-path calls submit, poll, and collect an attempt. A fourth operation requests cancellation and reports whether termination is confirmed. Refused requests also retain an identifier and a collectable record."}
submit:
  takes: typed request, submission_token
  returns: attempt_id, admission status (ADMITTED | REFUSED)
poll:
  takes: attempt_id
  returns: REFUSED | QUEUED | RUNNING | EVICTED | COMPLETED | FAILED | CANCELED
collect:
  takes: attempt_id
  returns: execution record (artifacts, parse status, cost, lineage)
cancel:
  takes: attempt_id
  returns: CONFIRMED after all attached work stops | UNCONFIRMED (quarantine)
```

Idempotency prevents duplicate work, but it does not limit the number of distinct requests. The capacity analysis in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization explains why a fast proposal method can overload a slower evaluation stage. The runtime responsibility is to enforce that capacity plan through admission limits, bounded queues, and backpressure, which asks the caller to slow or pause submissions. Capacity at one stage does not imply capacity at the next; available processors may still be waiting for licenses or dependent results.

::: {.callout-law title="Queueing Congestion Collapse in Tool Loops"}
**The Classical Principle:** In a queueing model with variable arrivals or service times, mean time in the system can grow without bound as arrival rate approaches service capacity ($W \to \infty$ as $\lambda \to \mu$) [@Kleinrock1975QueueingSystems]. Here $W$ includes waiting and execution time, $\lambda$ is the request arrival rate, and $\mu$ is the service rate.

**The Hardware Trap:** A generator proposes candidates faster than the available simulators and licensed tools can evaluate them. Without admission limits, the queue keeps growing. By the time a simulation finishes, upstream specifications, compiler branches, or interface assumptions may have moved. The result still describes its recorded inputs, but may no longer answer the active design question.

**The Architectural Antidote:** The execution harness must limit admitted work, throttling candidate generation as downstream utilization ($\rho = \lambda / \mu$) approaches capacity. Queue limits reduce the risk that results return after their input assumptions have become stale; they cannot guarantee freshness when tool durations or upstream changes are unpredictable (@sec-law-congestion-collapse in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).
:::

### Fault Containment and Execution Quarantines

Suppose a synthesis run reaches its time limit and the harness requests cancellation. The launcher exits, but a worker it started is still writing a design database. Reusing that workspace for a retry could mix files from two attempts. Fault containment limits the effect of this unfinished work on other executions. It requires control of the processes and writable resources belonging to an attempt, together with a way to determine whether they are still active.

On Linux, control groups (cgroups) can track a job's local processes together. The cgroup v2 `cgroup.kill` interface targets processes in a group and its descendants, while the group's status can indicate whether live processes remain.[^fn-process-containment-c06] The harness must arrange for the relevant workers to belong to the tracked groups and confirm that attached work has stopped before reclaiming its resources. Remote workers require corresponding control through their execution backend; terminating the local launcher does not establish that remote work has ended.

If termination cannot be confirmed, the harness places the affected execution in *quarantine*: its workspace remains separate, its outputs are not published as a completed result, and its uncertain allocations are not treated as available for new work. This is an enforced restriction on reuse, not merely a status label. A late write may still reach the old workspace, but it must not reach a retry's workspace or shared candidate artifacts. A retry can use a separate workspace and allocation when those boundaries and the remaining budget permit it. The quarantined attempt remains tracked until the harness resolves its execution state and can safely reclaim the affected resources.

Limits on model calls, tool submissions, compute time, memory, storage, and licenses constrain how much work an attempt can consume. They need mechanisms suited to each resource: a process limit does not establish license availability, and a submission limit does not bound a running tool's memory use. The license server's supported release mechanism must establish when a checkout is available again. Until then, the harness retains the unresolved allocation rather than inferring release from a cancellation request.

Recovery also has to preserve the study's accounting. A retry of the same design under the same tool settings retains its `candidate_id` and `configuration_id`, but receives a new attempt record. Any changed inputs or settings must be identified explicitly. Each attempt retains its outputs, measured resource use, and associated costs, including compute time, memory and storage use, and license occupancy. Costs that cannot yet be determined remain unknown rather than becoming zero. Human repair effort requires separate recording when the study includes it in the budget. These records let the method distinguish unfinished execution from a completed evaluation, but deciding how to recover also requires knowing what failed.

### Categorizing Tool and Environment Failures

A stopped or unsuccessful evaluation does not necessarily tell us that the candidate is a poor design. A FlexLM[^fn-flexlm-c06] license checkout denial means the tool could not acquire the requested license; a host out-of-memory failure means execution could not obtain the memory it needed. Neither establishes that the hardware is unroutable. If the environment records either event as a design failure, a predictor may learn the wrong label and an optimizer may discard a candidate that has not received the intended evaluation.

Recovery begins by separating what happened during execution from what the returned material says about the design. @tbl-failure-taxonomy lists nine conditions worth retaining. They can overlap: an infrastructure interruption may leave an incomplete report that also causes parsing to fail, while a completed timing analysis may report a constraint violation. Earlier successful evaluations of the candidate remain part of its history even when another attempt fails.

| **Recorded condition** | **How it appears** | **Preserved evidence** | **Runtime response** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Invalid request** | Illegal parameter or meaning-altering translation detected prior to invocation. | Request, validation rule, refusal reason. | Repair syntax only if meaning is preserved; otherwise refuse and return to caller. |
| **Setup / dependency failure** | Missing top-level, clock, library, constraint, or checkpoint. | Setup check, diagnostics, partial artifacts, cost. | Restore or regenerate required inputs; record which evaluation could not proceed. |
| **Infrastructure failure** | License server unreachable, host out-of-memory (OOM), scheduler preemption. | Execution record, failure source, cost, retry eligibility. | Retry if policy and resources permit; retain any partial observations and mark the interrupted evaluation incomplete. |
| **Tool failure** | Crash or tool-reported execution error, such as a gem5 crash or failed elaboration. | Tool diagnostics, exit code, partial artifacts, cost. | Inspect the diagnostic to distinguish tool malfunction, input problems, and reported design errors before choosing recovery. |
| **Incomplete return** | Missing or truncated report files. | Stage records, produced files, raw logs, parse status. | Recover retained files or regenerate missing outputs where possible; rerun only the required work. |
| **Parser failure** | An available report cannot be interpreted according to the expected schema; absent source data may also indicate an incomplete return. | Parser version, raw log, recognized tokens, residual output. | Check the report and parser version; repair parsing and reparse if the required source data is present. |
| **Formal-tool return** | SVA/BMC tool returns a proof, counterexample, bounded result, or unresolved outcome. | Original status, method, property, model, assumptions, bound, available proof or counterexample trace, cost. | Preserve the exact status and its scope, including any timeout or other reason the check remains unresolved. |
| **Reported limit violation** | Completed run reports physical violation (OpenROAD worst negative slack (WNS) $< 0$, DRC error). | Typed violation, units, conditions, raw report, cost. | Record complete return without marking run as tool failure. |
| **Complete tool return** | Expected artifacts exist and parse cleanly (including limit violations). | Typed metrics, units, conditions, warnings, raw logs, cost, lineage. | Retain return for measurement qualification. |
: **Execution status determines what ran, not what the architecture means.** Operational failures, partial returns, parser errors, and physical violations remain separate so recovery targets exact causes. {#tbl-failure-taxonomy tbl-colwidths="[20,24,28,28]"}

The distinction changes the next action. If a timing tool completed but a parser stopped recognizing its report format, reparsing the retained report may recover the result without another timing run. If the required library was missing, the inputs must be repaired before execution can answer the question. If a completed analysis reports negative slack, repeating the same run is not a remedy for that violation; the design, constraints, or interpretation need examination.

Formal results need similar care. A counterexample identifies a violation of the stated property in the supplied model, while a solver timeout leaves the question unresolved. A proof applies under its recorded assumptions, and bounded checking has a specified scope [@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. The harness should retain the tool's original status and supporting material alongside any normalized fields, so that a common interface does not erase these distinctions.

A clean report also has limits. Timing and physical checks depend on the tool version, libraries, operating corners, and applied exceptions. If an optimizer adds a false-path exception[^fn-false-path-c06] merely to suppress a timing violation, it has changed what is checked. Likewise, a timing analysis that omits dynamic IR drop[^fn-ir-drop-c06] cannot establish timing under that effect. The environment must retain these settings and analysis assumptions with the result. Raw reports, warnings, and unrecognized log lines remain useful when later review discovers that a parsed summary omitted something consequential.

### Caching and Artifact Reuse

Retained work can reduce the cost of the next evaluation. A compiled simulator may serve several candidates, a generated netlist may feed more than one analysis, and a complete raw report may be reparsed after a parser repair. Each case reuses a different artifact with different dependencies. The runtime question is whether that artifact still applies to the requested operation, not simply whether a file with the expected name exists.

A cache key identifies the inputs and settings used to produce an artifact. Relevant dependencies may include source contents, tool versions, PDK views, flags, workloads, and operating conditions. Identifying build outputs through their dependencies has precedent in the purely functional deployment model [@Dolstra2006Purely]. In a hardware flow, an omitted library corner or tool default can still make two apparently matching requests evaluate different conditions. A key is useful only to the extent that its dependencies describe the work being reused; a matching hash does not establish that a library is appropriate for the requested analysis.

Reuse also has to remain visible in the study's accounting. Returning a cached timing report supplies an existing observation, not an independent repeated measurement. The record should point to the producing attempt and distinguish the cost of retrieving the result from the original execution cost. For a generative step, retained model context is an input too. Context from a proprietary design must not silently enter an open-source baseline run; its reuse must follow the study's data-access and disclosure rules.

Resuming a checkpoint is different from retrieving a completed artifact: it continues execution from an intermediate state. The harness must identify the checkpoint's inputs, tool configuration, and execution history and establish that it is suitable for the intended continuation. A *reset*, by contrast, restores the starting state required by the next attempt. It may initialize a fresh workspace or restore a suitable baseline checkpoint. In either case, the tool databases, emulator memory, and other relevant mutable state must match that starting state. A soft reset that leaves memory buffers or peripheral registers unchanged is sufficient only if the study permits that retained state and records it.

Stopping a process does not itself perform a reset, and matching checkpoint hashes does not establish that restoration succeeded. License release is a separate resource-management operation, governed by the license server rather than regenerated from design inputs. When work runs again, the record identifies whether it started fresh or continued from retained state and preserves the cost of each execution segment without counting the same work twice. The stale-library example illustrates why this distinction between identity and suitability matters even for a seemingly simple cache hit.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The stale library view"}
**The claim.** In this illustrative failure, a design update reruns static timing analysis and receives a clean report indicating that the checked bus paths meet the requested clock period.

**The gap.** The analyzer loaded a cached library view that did not match the intended operating conditions. The report described checks under that stale view; it did not establish timing at the requested conditions.

**The lesson.** Before reusing a library view, the harness must check that it is the view required for the requested design and operating conditions. Checksums help identify PDK, LEF, and Liberty files, but compatibility also depends on their contents and intended use. A clean report from the wrong view cannot establish that the design meets timing under the intended conditions.
:::

### Design Drift and Execution Variability {#sec-incremental-churn-dispersion}

An evaluation may be reproducible for its recorded inputs while no longer answering the team's current design question. During a search against a fixed revision, other work may change compiler passes, runtime software, tool versions, or RTL interfaces. A candidate developed against snapshot $t_0$ may therefore need adaptation and reevaluation before it can be used at $t_0 + \Delta t$. The earlier result still describes its original configuration; it does not automatically transfer to the new one.

The practical question is how much work must be repeated after a change. Regenerating an entire accelerator and repeating physical synthesis for every register or arbiter change can make a search too slow for daily engineering work. A harness can use structural information, such as CIRCT representations, Chisel module hierarchies, and dependency-graph build systems such as Bazel, to identify artifacts affected under its declared dependencies. Reusing other artifacts depends on those dependencies being complete. A file or module boundary alone does not establish that a simulation result or formal conclusion remains valid.

Physical implementation makes that limitation concrete. In flattened placement and routing, a local register change can alter congestion, clock-tree structure, and routing elsewhere. Hierarchical partitioning may limit the work to repeat when its interface, timing, and physical assumptions still hold. The harness records the basis for reuse and the work repeated when upstream changes invalidate assumptions. It also tracks changes between an active search snapshot and the mainline, so the study can stop, resynchronize, or repeat affected work under a declared policy.

Revision changes are distinct from variation across repeated executions of the same configuration. To interpret that variation, the environment must keep three mechanisms separate:

- **Host runtime jitter.** CPU frequency changes, NUMA migration, memory contention, and storage contention can change elapsed time and tool throughput without changing the simulated guest cycle count of a deterministic run. Records preserve the host placement, governor, storage path, and other declared runtime conditions.
- **Explicit algorithmic randomness.** Generative methods, stochastic search passes, and randomized EDA stages can produce different candidates, layouts, or metrics. Records preserve seeds where the implementation exposes them, along with sampling and algorithm settings. Unavailable randomness controls must be recorded as a limitation.
- **Parallel execution nondeterminism.** Some tools can return different artifacts or metrics when thread counts or execution schedules change. Records preserve thread and concurrency settings rather than assuming that pinning removes this source of variation.

A randomized placement stage can return different layouts and power, performance, and area metrics even when the RTL and architecture remain fixed. Its best result may be a useful implementation worth retaining. That result alone, however, does not show that the architecture consistently outperforms an alternative under comparable evaluation effort. If an optimizer retains only favorable outcomes, later analysis cannot distinguish an architectural improvement from a favorable execution of the tool.

The study therefore needs to specify how repeated evaluations fit its budget and retain their settings, outcomes, failures, and costs. Recording a seed does not eliminate variation from parallel execution, nor do repeated runs automatically justify a particular statistical model. @sec-feedback-verification-trust explains how to assess whether the observations support a confidence interval, a matched comparison, or candidate advancement. The environment's role is to preserve the information needed for that assessment in the execution records described next.

## Execution Records {#sec-execution-records}

The execution record brings together the information needed to answer three questions: what work was attempted, what happened, and what can be examined afterward? @sec-architecture-20-ontology introduced its role in connecting requested work to the state actually evaluated. Here it consolidates the identities, outputs, and costs developed throughout the chapter. A refused request needs a record even though no tool ran; an attempt with several backend jobs needs their outcomes linked together. A later successful retry adds to this history rather than replacing it.

Six groups of information make the record useful:

- **Request and attempt identity**: Study, request, run specification, candidate, configuration, workload, attempt universally unique identifier (UUID), submission token, and attached scheduler job identifiers.
- **Starting state**: Input artifacts, source revisions, tool and container versions, library views, and operating conditions.
- **Execution outcome**: Admission status, job outcomes, terminal cause, artifact completeness, parser status, and recovery eligibility.
- **Returned material**: Raw reports and logs, artifact references and hashes, structured metrics with units and scope, warnings, and unrecognized output.
- **Lineage and retries**: Dependencies, producing transformations, and links to earlier attempts or restored checkpoints, with references to any checks performed.
- **Resource use and cost**: Wall-clock time, CPU/accelerator hours, peak memory, storage use, license-hours, and charges, distinguishing measured values from estimates or unknowns.

The excerpt in @lst-execution-record-schema illustrates a completed analysis that reports a timing violation. All identifiers, artifact references, metrics, and costs are invented teaching values; this is not an executed Lighthouse result. A generic licensed analysis tool is used so the example does not imply that a particular product produced every metric. Workload and activity references identify the inputs relevant to the power estimate, while the scope identifies what that estimate covers. The excerpt remains abbreviated: a complete record would also retain full input identities, host settings, per-job details, and applicable retry or checkpoint links.

```{.yaml #lst-execution-record-schema lst-cap="**A completed analysis can report a timing violation.** This hypothetical excerpt joins inputs and conditions to execution status, reports, metrics, and costs. Values are invented; this is neither a complete schema nor an executed Lighthouse result."}
study_id: "lighthouse-xr-soc-v1"
evidence_status: "HYPOTHETICAL_TEACHING_EXAMPLE"
request_id: "req-illustrative-0417"
attempt_id: "att-8f3a91c2-7b1e"
submission_token: "tok-lighthouse-0417"
scheduler_jobs: ["slurm-4471902"]
candidate_id: "cand-l2-3mib-npu16x16"
configuration_id: "cfg-illustrative-0417"
workload_id: "xr-workload-illustrative-v1"
starting_state:
  git_commit: "9a2f1b4c"
  container_digest: "sha256:d4e7b1a8c9e..."
  tool_version: "illustrative-licensed-analysis-tool-v1"
  library_view: "illustrative-library-corner-v1"
  netlist: "artifact-netlist-0417"
  constraints: "artifact-constraints-0417"
  activity: "artifact-activity-0417"
  power_scope: "modeled XR subsystem"
outcome:
  admission_status: "ADMITTED"
  status: "COMPLETED"
  terminal_cause: "NORMAL_EXIT"
  exit_code: 0
  artifact_status: "REQUIRED_OUTPUTS_PRESENT"
  parser_status: "PARSED"

  timing: "artifact-timing-report-0417"
  area: "artifact-area-report-0417"
  power: "artifact-power-report-0417"
  raw_log: "artifact-log-0417"

  worst_negative_slack_ps: -12.4
  macro_area_mm2: 1.42
